name: Adapalene
summary: A topical retinoid used for comedonal and mild inflammatory acne because it is effective, generally well tolerated, and easy to pair with benzoyl peroxide.
good: Maintenance and early acne control, especially comedones.
bad: Irritated or over-exfoliated skin without barrier repair.
clinicalPearls: It works best as a long-game prevention drug, not as an instant spot fix.
mechanism: Retinoid receptor modulation normalizes keratinization and helps prevent microcomedone formation.
indications: Comedonal acne, mild inflammatory acne, and maintenance after improvement.
interactionNotes: Layering with harsh exfoliants or over-frequent cleansing can worsen barrier disruption.

warnings: Dryness, peeling, and irritation are the practical limiting effects.

Comedonal and mild inflammatory acne; the default starting retinoid, widely available over the counter at 0.1%.
Slow, similar 8–12 week timeline to tretinoin, but the initial purge/irritation phase is typically milder.
Lower than tretinoin — more photostable and chemically stable, generally the best-tolerated topical retinoid.
Same turnover-driven PIH benefit as tretinoin, with lower risk of irritation-triggered pigmentation along the way.
Milder barrier disruption than tretinoin, though still present, especially in the first few weeks.
Night preferred; more UV-stable than tretinoin, but nighttime application remains standard practice.
More oxidation-stable than tretinoin, so it pairs cleanly with benzoyl peroxide — fixed-dose adapalene/BPO combination gels are a first-line evidence-based standard for mild-moderate acne.
